The shipped planner returns an error on a query failure, main exits 1 and writes no report, and evaluate_scenario then `continue`s past every per-order check — so the §4-specific branch of `authorization_applied` (the `wanted["authorization"] is None` case) and the INDETERMINATE branch of `authorization_source` never execute at all on the baseline. refuted.why_refuted:
REFUTED. Every quoted line is real, and I reproduced the auditor's numbers exactly — but the conclusion ("CHECK_SECTIONS mis-attributes §4", "declared sections are swapped", "the section registry records the wrong correspondence") does not follow.

WHAT CHECKS OUT
- /Users/devlegacy/Desktop/projects/ai-gap-coverage-projects/agent-eval-foundry/tasks/caa-revalidation-repair/tests/checks.py:26-37 has CHECK_SECTIONS with "report_present": "6" and "authorization_applied": "2,3,4"; :164-173 has the two `fail("report_present", ...); continue` guards; environment/app/certd/internal/authz/planner.go:85-87 returns the error; cmd/certd/main.go:61-64 propagates it to os.Exit(1). All verbatim.
- Only tests/scenarios/selected/sel-13.json has a non-empty `fail_with` in the graded suite (tests/test_certd.py:12 grades suite=="selected" only). In sel-13, o1 is all-cache (d's stored age is exactly 8h, current per §2), and o2 crashes.
- I replayed the shipped planner over all 24 selected scenarios against checks.evaluate_scenario. Per-check scenario failure counts: report_present 1 (sel-13, "o2: exit 1, report absent"), outcome 9, authorization_applied 21, store_recorded 21, other six 0 — identical to the auditor's table. No authorization_applied failure carries the §4 message. So the narrow observation "the §4 branch never executes on the shipped baseline" is TRUE.

WHY THE CLAIM STILL FAILS

1. Category error about what CHECK_SECTIONS is. The checks.py docstring says each check "names the section ... it enforces" — a coverage registry over the space of submissions, not a prediction about which check trips on one particular buggy binary. tests/test_certd.py:34-40 asserts only that the union of declared sections == {2,3,4,5,6,7,9} and that keys == CHECK_IDS. It never asserts baseline-firing correspondence, so nothing "blessed" by it is falsified.

2. authorization_applied demonstrably IS the §4 enforcer. I replayed the natural near-miss — pairing fixed, query error handled as a "fail-safe" FORBID (source AUTHORITY). Over selected, the only failing checks are:
   authorization_applied: "o2: d.example.test carries FORBID, but no authorization was established for it"
   authorization_source: "d.example.test sourced AUTHORITY, expected INDETERMINATE"
   store_recorded: "d.example.test established at ...21:00:00Z, expected ...04:00:00Z"
   Same with PERMIT. Changing only that to INDETERMINATE scores clean (zero failures). That is the `wanted["authorization"] is None` branch firing, failing, with the §4 message, and being fatal. The check does enforce §4 for every submission where §4 is the live question.

3. No swap. report_present is mapped to §6 and fires for a §6 violation in §6's own words — environment/app/spec/SEMANTICS.md:73: "Every well-formed order produces a report and exits zero, whatever the outcome." The baseline's abandonment violates that sentence directly. §4's "does not abandon the order" (SEMANTICS.md:49-50) and §6:73 describe the same observable; the spec states it twice. Overlapping obligations, not mis-assigned ones. report_present is not standing in for §4 — it is enforcing §6's own text on conduct that happens to also violate §4.

4. The auditor's criterion, applied consistently, would condemn most of the registry. authorization_applied is also mapped to §2, and §2 never fires on the baseline either: `diff environment/app/certd/internal/authz/cache.go tests/reference/certd/internal/authz/cache.go` differs only by the canary header, so the baseline commits no freshness violation at all. `outcome` (§5) fires 9 times purely as a downstream consequence of §3 mispairing, not from an issuance-rule bug. By this standard §2 and §5 would be "mis-attributed" too. The standard is wrong, not the mapping.

5. The claim itself concedes there is no exploit and reward is 0. The shipped planner is byte-identical (modulo canary header) to tests/mutants/identity-collapse/internal/authz/planner.go, whose declared INTENDED check in tests/gate.py:35 is authorization_applied — and it fires on 21/24, so gate.py's every_mutant_independently_fatal control holds for the shipped defect as declared. | The claim holds on every checkable assertion, including the exact counts.

1. CHECK_SECTIONS mapping — confirmed at /Users/devlegacy/Desktop/projects/ai-gap-coverage-projects/agent-eval-foundry/tasks/caa-revalidation-repair/tests/checks.py: `"authorization_applied": "2,3,4"`. It is the ONLY check naming section 4 (report_present:6, outcome:5, decisions_cover_identifiers:6, authorization_source:6, store_recorded:3, audit_matches_report:7, rechecked_exactly_the_stale:"2,3", rechecks_issued_together:3, no_unnamed_or_late_query:"3,9").

2. The abandonment path — confirmed in environment/app/certd/internal/authz/planner.go: `if result.err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("recheck %s: %w", name, result.err) }`. In environment/app/certd/cmd/certd/main.go, `run()` returns that error before `st.Save()`, `order.SaveReport` and `audit.Write`, and `main` does `os.Exit(1)`. No report, no audit, no store write.

3. The skip — confirmed in tests/checks.py `evaluate_scenario`: `if actual.get("exit_code") != 0 or not isinstance(report, dict) or "__unreadable__" in report: fail("report_present", ...); continue`. The `continue` is inside the per-order loop, so it bypasses outcome, decisions_cover_identifiers, authorization_applied, authorization_source, store_recorded, audit_matches_report, rechecked_exactly_the_stale and rechecks_issued_together for that order. refuted.title: `Pending.Position` is computed with the correct index and never read — the buggy code carries its own fix
refuted.claim: planner.go declares a `Pending` struct whose entire purpose is to carry `Position`, populates it with the correct order index at line 42, passes it into `Reconcile`, and then never reads it. The assembly loop instead uses a bare `used++` counter. A struct field that is set and never consumed, in a 96-line file, is the single loudest possible signal that the assembly is supposed to be indexed and isn't — and it tells the reader not merely that there is a bug but exactly what the repair is (index the answers by `Position`, or key them by `Name`). The agent-visible unit test suite compounds this by asserting the field's semantics that the production code ignores.
refuted.why_refuted:
The auditor's quoted line-level evidence is literally accurate, but the consequence does not follow — the claim is refuted on four independent grounds.

VERIFIED AS QUOTED (all true):
- /Users/devlegacy/Desktop/projects/ai-gap-coverage-projects/agent-eval-foundry/tasks/caa-revalidation-repair/environment/app/certd/internal/authz/planner.go:29-32 declares `type Pending struct { Position int; Name string }`; :42 populates `Pending{Position: i, Name: name}`; :60-63 the goroutine closes over `item.Name` only; :83-84 is `result := rechecked[used]` / `used++`.
- `grep -rn Position environment/` returns exactly 5 hits: planner.go:30, planner.go:42, and planner_test.go:184/198/199. Position is indeed never read in non-test code, and planner_test.go:184-200 is `TestPendingIsOrderedByOrderPosition` asserting `pending[0].Position != 0 || pending[1].Position != 2`.

WHY THE CLAIM IS STILL FALSE:

1. Position is set-and-never-read in the CORRECT code too, so it cannot be a signal about the defect. tests/reference/certd/internal/authz/planner.go (the graded reference repair) keeps the identical struct at :32 and the identical population at :44 and reads Position nowhere. solution/files/internal/authz/planner.go is byte-identical to the reference (diff → IDENTICAL). All nine mutant overlays carry the same unused field, including tests/mutants/alt-reference/internal/authz/planner.go — a second, independently-written CORRECT implementation, which also sets Position at :42 and never reads it, carrying identity on the wire via a `settled{name, answer}` struct instead. A field that is unused before the repair, after the repair, and in an alternative correct repair is stable exported API surface (with an agent-visible test defending the documented "in the order they appear on the order" contract of the Pending method), not a vestige of the bug. The auditor's whole inference rests on "set and never consumed ⇒ the consumption is the missing fix"; the fixed tree falsifies the premise.

2. The repair the auditor says the field prescribes is wrong and would panic. "Index the answers by Position" cannot work: `rechecked` holds len(pending) entries indexed 0..len(pending)-1, while Position indexes ord.Identifiers. On the very test the auditor cites, pending[1].Position == 2 with len(pending) == 2 → index out of range. The reference fix uses a separate slot index `i` for the answers slice (planner.go:62-68) and keys the lookup map by Name (:72-75, :88). Followed literally, the field points away from the fix, not at it.

3. The surviving alternative ("key them by Name") is not learned from the field — it is published normatively and in bold in the agent-visible spec. environment/app/spec/SEMANTICS.md §3: "The authorization applied to an identifier is the one the authority gave **for that identifier**," immediately preceded by "It serves queries concurrently, and the order in which its answers arrive is not the order in which they were asked." instruction.md:16 restates it, and SEMANTICS.md:5 declares the document normative and authoritative over the code. The pairing requirement is deliberately disclosed contract, so an unused struct field cannot be "the single loudest possible signal" — the loudest signal is the spec, by design.

4. The claim covers at most half the defect and adds nothing beyond the contract. Position says nothing about defect #2 (query error returns nil and abandons the order instead of emitting INDETERMINATE). That half is also published (SEMANTICS.md §4 "does not abandon the order"; instruction.md:20) and is graded: tests/checks.py CHECK_SECTIONS maps authorization_applied → sections "2,3,4", plus outcome, audit_matches_report, store_recorded, rechecked_exactly_the_stale, rechecks_issued_together, no_unnamed_or_late_query. The claimed exploit ("grep -rn Position alone, with no reading of the algorithm") yields none of the INDETERMINATE behaviour, none of the cross-order store persistence, and none of the single-round-trip concurrency requirement, so it does not produce a passing repair.

Net: the observation is real but inert. It is a cosmetic property shared by the buggy, reference, solution, and alt-reference trees; the fix it allegedly prescribes is a panic; and the information it allegedly leaks is already normative published contract that the task intends the agent to read. This does not explain the fast frontier-agent solves. | All load-bearing factual assertions of the claim hold, verified directly against the files.

CONFIRMED (environment/app/certd/internal/authz/planner.go, exactly 96 lines per wc -l):
- Lines 29-32 declare `type Pending struct { Position int; Name string }`.
- Line 42 populates it with the true document index: `pending = append(pending, Pending{Position: i, Name: name})`, where `i` is the range index over ord.Identifiers. The line number in the claim is exact.
- Line 56 `pending := p.Pending(ord, now)` brings those values into Reconcile; line 59-63 iterate them and consume only `item.Name`.
- Lines 72/83/84 are the bare positional counter: `used := 0` ... `result := rechecked[used]` / `used++`.
- Exhaustive `grep -rn "Position"` over the whole task tree: the ONLY reads of `.Position` anywhere are in the two planner_test.go files (environment + tests/reference). No production file -- not cmd/certd/main.go, not internal/audit/writer.go, not tests/reference/, not solution/files/, not any of the 12 mutants -- ever reads it. The field is set and never consumed, exactly as claimed.
- environment/app/certd/internal/authz/planner_test.go:184-201 `TestPendingIsOrderedByOrderPosition` asserts `pending[0].Position != 0 || pending[1].Position != 2`. It is agent-visible and passes on the defective code (Pending() itself is correct), so the visible suite does assert the field's semantics that Reconcile ignores. The "compounds this" sub-claim holds.

No line stops anyone from using this hint, and there is no exploit here to stop -- this is a discoverability/leakage claim, and the repair it points toward is the intended repair, so the verifier has no reason to block it. minor.title: Query events are attributed to orders by count in tick order, ignoring the event's own scenario/order provenance
minor.claim: `partition_queries` sorts the authority log by tick and slices it into per-order buckets by expected pending count, with no reference to the `scenario` field the authority stamps on each event. The authority records an event only after its `delay_ms` sleep, so any query still in flight when certd exits lands in the log after the next order's exec has already begun (next-exec latency is roughly 5-15 ms; delays run to 100 ms). The straggler is then charged to the following order and that order's real first event is charged backwards, so which of `rechecked_exactly_the_stale` / `no_unnamed_or_late_query` fails becomes timing-dependent. Correct submissions are unaffected (they must wait for every answer before building decisions, and the authority records before it replies), and submissions that abandon queries fail on other grounds anyway — but the failure reason is not reproducible. Separately, a straggler recorded in the window between `dump` and the next `arm` is silently discarded by `del _EVENTS[:]`, a few-millisecond hole in the "append-only, nothing drains it" record.

Not exploitable for reward, but it makes the recorded failure reason for such a submission non-reproducible.

minor.claim: The two headline worries under this lens do not hold up. Scheduler luck cannot flip the verdict for the intended defect or for a correct repair: every graded multi-pending order contains at least one query pair with a >=50 ms overlap window, and every completion-order inversion has a >=40 ms margin, two to three orders of magnitude above Python thread-dispatch jitter. Evidence does not leak between scenarios: `arm` clears the event list and replaces policy, delays and failures wholesale; an identifier not named by the armed scenario is refused and logged as `unnamed_query`; any extra query becomes `leftover`; and a query answered after `seal` becomes `late_query`. All three feed `no_unnamed_or_late_query`, so a process that survived `killpg` (e.g. via its own `setsid()`) and polled the authority to pre-learn a later scenario's policy would convict itself in the log. `start_new_session=True` plus `os.killpg(proc.pid, ...)` is correctly targeted, and `communicate()` blocks until the stdout/stderr pipes close, so ordinary children cannot outlive their order.

lensSummaries.summary: FATAL verifier bypass found and reproduced end-to-end. A submission can score reward=1 without performing the intended repair. Mechanism: the agent's /app/certd is an arbitrary Go binary that the grader compiles (offline, stdlib-only, passing all anti-cheat) and executes as user `nobody` during collection (tests/collect.py). The scoring pytest process is ALSO run as `nobody` with HOME=/tmp/pytest-work and no -s/PYTHONNOUSERSITE (tests/test.sh:89), so CPython auto-imports `usercustomize` from /tmp/pytest-work/.local/lib/python3.11/site-packages/. certd, running earlier as the same uid on world-writable /tmp, creates that path and drops a usercustomize.py; test.sh's later `mkdir -p ... && chown` is non-recursive and does not remove it. At pytest startup the attacker code monkeypatches checks.evaluate_scenario to all-pass and checks.completion_inverted to True, so all 243 derived checks pass, pytest-json-ctrf writes a legitimate CTRF with the exact derived count and allowed names, and the root final gate writes reward=1 (test.sh:103-120). The payload is pure stdlib (os.MkdirAll+os.WriteFile), matches none of the three anti-cheat source tokens, and needs no vendor/go.work/replace, no access to the authority's private log/socket, and no knowledge of the hidden scenarios. Reproduced in golang:1.25-bookworm (python 3.11.2) against the real tests/checks.py and tests/test_certd.py, mirroring every relevant line of test.sh: pytest exit=0, 13/13 CTRF passed, REWARD -> 1, while certd emitted only {\"garbage\":true} reports. Root cause: the grader and the untrusted binary share the same uid and a HOME-derived Python import path under world-writable /tmp; the design's 'different privilege levels' guarantee protects the authority log but not the asserting process. Fixes: run pytest with python3 -S -E / PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1, or as a distinct uid, or from a fresh HOME under a root-only 0700 directory certd cannot write. This plausibly explains a clean/fast solve only if an agent went looking for the channel; it does not by itself prove the two frontier agents cheated, but it is a real reward-1-without-repair path. Also reported: two supporting informational/minor notes on the isolation framing and the narrow, source-only anti-cheat. Not a null result. The agent-visible package contains a working reproducer for BOTH halves of the intended defect, in the shipped harness scenarios that instruction.md explicitly tells the agent to run. (1) `scenarios/refused-order` has two identifiers that are both stale at the scenario's `now` and whose authority answers differ (shop=PERMIT, old=FORBID) — exactly the activation condition the README says the visible harness cannot express — and it reproduces the mispairing on ~38% of unmodified runs (measured 77/200 at cpus=2, and reproduced through the shipped `run-scenario.sh` itself, which prints the swapped report AND the swapped store-after). (2) `scenarios/authority-unavailable` deterministically demonstrates the second defect: `exit 1` and `--- report --- (none)`, in flat contradiction of SEMANTICS.md sections 4 and 6. Both findings contradict the task's central difficulty premise that "the natural way to reproduce the problem locally does not reproduce it" and that the five scenarios "all produce the report a reader would expect", and they plausibly explain the ~5-minute frontier-agent solve. Supporting minor leaks: instruction.md asserts a falsehood about the scenarios, and three dead affordances in visible code (`order.Indeterminate` declared but referenced nowhere in shipped certd; `Decision.Detail` never set; `Pending.Position` computed and unit-tested but never consumed by Reconcile) each point straight at the two missing behaviours. The built agent image is otherwise clean: no git dirs, no .orig/.rej/.bak/.swp files, no compiled binaries, no reference or verifier material, no TODO/FIXME markers; shipped tests pass, `go vet` is clean, and `go test -race` is clean.

Null result on the headline question: I could not find a check-soundness hole that lets a wrong repair pass. expected_orders() is a faithful clause-for-clause replay of SEMANTICS.md §2-§6 (inclusive 8h boundary, cached entries keep their original checked_at, rechecks written back at the evaluation time, indeterminate records nothing and does not abandon, conjunctive outcome, document ordering), and every graded behaviour has a published basis. Nothing in the graded oracle is soft: a pairing-only repair fails sel-13 on report_present, an error-path-only repair fails 21 scenarios, and a serialised repair fails rechecks_issued_together on all 24 plus test_mechanism_fired_somewhere. The task's difficulty does not come from the checks being weak.

What I did find is that the suite carries substantially less independent signal than "ten obligations x twenty-four scenarios" advertises, and that the package's headline rigour claim is not implemented. I simulated the shipped planner (verified byte-identical to the identity-collapse mutant) against all 24 graded scenarios: it fails 52 of 240 assertions, concentrated in four checks, of which store_recorded fails on exactly the same 21 scenarios as authorization_applied (both derive from the same mispaired `result` variable) and outcome's 9 failures are a strict subset that provably cannot occur in order 1 (permuting answers within an order permutes a multiset; measured 0 order-1 mismatches, 9 order-2). Six of the ten checks never fire at all. Two graded scenarios, sel-02 and sel-18, are provably non-activating by construction — the mispair either does not happen (delay order equals document order) or swaps two identical PERMIT answers — which contradicts select.py's own discriminates() gate that required identity-collapse to fail every selected point.

The three material findings: (1) test_every_obligation_is_checked, cited in README and task.toml as asserting spec-to-check correspondence "mechanically", never opens SEMANTICS.md — it compares a hardcoded literal against a hardcoded dict, is constant-true for every submission, and demonstrably does not catch the published-but-ungraded rule in §6 ("A malformed order produces no report and exits non-zero"); (2) CHECK_SECTIONS attributes §4 to authorization_applied, but on the shipped defect §4 is caught only by report_present (mapped to §6), and report_present's `continue` means the §4 branches of authorization_applied and authorization_source never execute at all; (3) the sel-02/sel-18 vacuity. Minor: audit_matches_report is a tautology for anything that leaves audit/writer.go alone; rechecks_issued_together — the only guard against a serialised repair, and the only timing-dependent oracle — has no validating mutant in gate.py even though mutex-serialized and serial-repair sit built-but-ungraded on disk, which is exactly the standard gate.py's own docstring sets.

LENS VERDICT: mostly a null result. Of the five partial repairs named in the brief, none passes the shipped verifier — each is caught, usually on many scenarios. I verified this by replaying every candidate through the real `tests/checks.py` (my replay reproduces "reference passes all 240 assertions" and "shipped defect fails" as a control).

Per-candidate results against the 24 frozen `tests/scenarios/selected/` scenarios (24 x 10 = 240 graded assertions; test.sh requires all to pass):

Pairing fixed, store write-back dropped -> FAILS. `store_recorded` on 24/24 (checks.py:230-233 `_store_matches`, e.g. "sel-01: o1: a.example.test established at 2031-03-03T12:00:00Z, expected 2031-03-04T12:00:00Z"), plus `authorization_source` on 11/24 (order 2 expects CACHE, gets AUTHORITY) and `no_unnamed_or_late_query` on 11/24 (the re-queries land in `leftover`, checks.py:257-264).

2. Pairing fixed, still abandons the order on a query error -> FAILS, but on exactly one scenario and one check: `report_present` on sel-13 ("o2: exit 1, report absent", checks.py:172-178, because main.go returns the error and never writes a report). 23/24 scenarios pass. See finding 1.

3. Error path fixed, pairing not fixed -> FAILS. `authorization_applied` on 22/24 (checks.py:204-210, e.g. "sel-01: o1: c.example.test applied PERMIT, the authority gave FORBID"), `store_recorded` 22/24, `outcome` 9/24, `authorization_source` on sel-13.

4. Answers sorted by name, consumed positionally -> FAILS. `authorization_applied` on 12/24, `store_recorded` 12/24, `outcome` 6/24. (This is exactly `tests/mutants/completion-order-association/`.)

5. Map keyed by name but populated in the wrong place -> FAILS. Populated in receive order it is identical to case 3 (22/24). Populated by `ord.Identifiers[i]` instead of `pending[i].Name` it still fails `authorization_applied` + `store_recorded` on 4/24 and `outcome` on 1/24 (the zero-value `answer` produces an empty authorization).

Two additional partials I tested: serial/`sync.Mutex`-gated queries with everything else correct -> FAILS `rechecks_issued_together` on 24/24 plus `test_mechanism_fired_somewhere`; error mapped to source=AUTHORITY instead of INDETERMINATE, and errgroup-style cancel-siblings-on-first-error -> both FAIL, but again only on sel-13.

The three things worth the owner's attention are below: all graded coverage of the second half of the defect rests on one order in one scenario (and the selection pipeline actively tries to delete exactly that input); a bounded worker pool of 2 satisfies the concurrency check on every graded order; and the two mutant overlays that model the authors' "part (a) without part (b)" claim are built but never scored by the integrity gate.

LENS VERDICT: the defect is highly legible from a cold read. The ~5-minute frontier solve is the expected outcome, not an anomaly, and the 6-hour expert estimate in task.toml is not supported by the agent-visible surface.

MINIMUM PATH: two hops. (1) Read instruction.md / SEMANTICS.md — three of the eight invariants are phrased as violations ('the one the authority gave for that identifier', 'recorded against the identifier it was performed for', 'does not abandon the order'), so both hypotheses form before any file is opened. (2) Open /app/certd/internal/authz/planner.go. Both defects are in one 42-line function. A third 'step' — recognizing the fan-in idiom — is a pattern match, not a derivation. There is a zero-inference variant that skips step 1 entirely: `grep -rn 'go func' /app/certd` returns exactly one hit in the whole service (planner.go:60); so does `grep -rn 'chan '`. Search space: 833 lines total, 96 in the planner, no decoy defects anywhere (cache.go's `<=` boundary, decider.go's conjunction, the store and audit writers are all correct), so nothing is spent on false leads.

LINES THAT MAKE IT VISIBLE: planner.go:48-51 (`answer` struct with authorization and err and no identifier); :60-63 (the closure has `name` in scope and pointedly does not send it); :66-69 (`for range pending { rechecked = append(rechecked, <-answers) }` — completion order); :83-84 (`result := rechecked[used]; used++` — document order); :85-87 (error returns nil, which main.go:61-64 turns into exit 1 with no report). And the loudest line of all, :42 vs :83 — `Pending{Position: i, Name: name}` computes the correct index and `Reconcile` never reads it. `grep -rn Position /app/certd` shows the field is read only by the agent-visible test suite.

DOES THE CODE SHAPE ANNOUNCE IT? Yes, unambiguously, to any reader who knows Go, spec or no spec. A keyless result type over a fan-out of named things, drained in receive order, consumed by position, is one of the most recognized Go antipatterns, and all three constructs sit within 35 lines. The second defect needs no analysis at all — it is a bare `return nil, err` where the spec says report and refuse.

DOES SEMANTICS.md COMPLETE THE DERIVATION? Yes, twice over. §3:26-27 asserts the required pairing in bold and §3:33-35 asserts, three lines later, that answers do not arrive in the order they were asked — precondition and postcondition in consecutive sentences, which reduces 'discover a concurrency hazard' to 'check one property'. §4:45-52 names the second defect's failure mode outright ('does not abandon the order') and §6:73 supplies the falsifier for the current behaviour.

WHICH ARTIFACT DOES THE MOST WORK: planner.go itself, and specifically the dead `Position` field. The spec tells you what must be true; the code tells you it isn't and hands you the fix. SEMANTICS.md §3 is a close second and removes all remaining doubt. Removing the spec sentence would barely slow a Go reader; removing the `Position` field and giving the answer struct a plausible reason to be keyless is what would actually make this hard.

TWO AUTHORIAL CLAIMS DO NOT SURVIVE CONTACT WITH THE SHIPPED PACKAGE. (a) 'all five scenarios produce the report a reader would expect' — false: `run-scenario.sh scenarios/authority-unavailable` deterministically prints `exit 1` and `(none)` for the report, a one-command demonstration of defect #2 against SEMANTICS.md:73. (b) 'the stand-in answers immediately and therefore in request order, so an engineer gets a green run over a broken service' — nothing synchronizes anything: devauthority serves each connection in its own goroutine and certd dials per-identifier from separate goroutines, and `refused-order` is the one scenario with two stale identifiers whose answers differ (PERMIT vs FORBID, no delay), so it is a coin flip that prints the swapped pairing in both the report and the 'store after' dump. I could not execute it — no Go toolchain on this box — so I claim only that the run is unsynchronized, not that it flips at a particular rate.

IN FAIRNESS: one repair decision is genuinely under-determined by the visible surface — `Decision.Authorization` lacks `omitempty` in the read-only order.go, so an INDETERMINATE decision serializes as `"authorization": ""` unless the agent adds a marshaller. That is verification cost, not discovery cost. Nothing here is a leak of the verifier or a degenerate-pass; this lens found no such thing, and did not look. The finding is narrower and blunter: locating this defect is a two-hop, sub-five-minute exercise for a strong Go reader, and the package hands over the fix as well as the bug.

Not a null result, but the harness's *timing* design — the part the lens most suspected — is sound. Grading of the intended defect is deterministic by construction (fuzz.py enforces MIN_DELAY_GAP_MS = 40; the smallest overlap window in any graded order is 50 ms), cross-scenario evidence leakage is closed by arm/seal plus the unnamed/late/leftover query traps, and the setpriv + process-group isolation of the control socket is genuine. Scenario coverage of the primary mispairing defect is deep: 22 of 24 selected scenarios have an order with 2+ pending identifiers whose delays invert completion order and whose answers differ, so the bug cannot hide.

Two findings do matter. First, the isolation is filesystem-blind: /tests is world-readable in the verifier image (it must be — pytest runs as `nobody` with PYTHONPATH=/tests), certd runs as `nobody` with no mount namespace or seccomp, and collect.py names each workdir after the hidden scenario id and passes that path to the binary as --store/--order/--report/--audit. A submission that keeps the mispairing bug, still fires the same concurrent queries, and reads answers out of /tests/scenarios/selected/<id>.json passes all 10 checks. gate.py's witness_isolation() probes only the control socket and challenge_nonleakage() scans only what the agent sees at solve time, so neither control covers this. Second, 5 of the 10 graded checks have no mutant witness in gate.py's INTENDED map, and the worst gap is `rechecks_issued_together` (SEMANTICS §3's round-trip clause): tests/mutants/serial-repair and tests/mutants/mutex-serialized are exactly the witnesses it needs, they are built by build-variants.sh, and gate.py never grades them.

Secondary notes: coverage is concentrated at single points off the main axis — one scenario (sel-13) grades the whole INDETERMINATE obligation, two orders guard against reversal-based repairs, and the graded suite never fans out past 3 pending identifiers though the grammar declares 5. The balanced suite runs on every submission without being graded (doubling execs and exposure), the controls suite never runs in the verifier at all, and checks.partition_queries attributes queries by count in tick order without consulting each event's own scenario stamp, which makes the failure reason non-reproducible for submissions that abandon in-flight queries.

interpretation:
This audit materially revises what the Phase 18 campaign can claim. Three findings matter most.

**(1) A fatal verifier bypass exists and was reproduced end to end.** The submitted service is compiled from the agent's own code and executed as `nobody` during collection; the scoring pytest runs later as the SAME uid with `HOME=/tmp/pytest-work` and without `-s` or `PYTHONNOUSERSITE`, so CPython auto-imports `usercustomize` from the HOME-derived user-site directory. The service can create that directory on world-writable /tmp before test.sh creates it, and test.sh's later `mkdir -p ... && chown` is non-recursive. The injected module monkeypatches `checks.evaluate_scenario` to all-pass, producing a legitimate CTRF with exactly the root-derived count and only whitelisted names, so the final root gate writes reward 1. The payload is pure stdlib and matches none of the anti-cheat greps. This is a B3 verifier bypass and it invalidates the package as a shippable benchmark task.

**(2) The package leaked a working reproducer of both defects.** The agent-visible harness scenario `refused-order` carries two identifiers that are both stale with differing authority answers - the exact activation condition the README claims the visible harness cannot express - and reproduces the mispairing on roughly 38% of unmodified runs (measured 77/200). `authority-unavailable` demonstrates the second defect deterministically, and its directory name announces the condition. instruction.md tells the agent to run these scenarios. This is a B2 package leak and it is the most economical explanation of the five-minute solves.

**(3) The defect was highly legible independently of the leak.** Two hops from instruction.md to both defects, both inside one 42-line function, in a 96-line file, in an 833-line service with no decoy defects. `grep -rn 'go func'` returns exactly one hit in the whole service; so does `grep -rn 'chan '`.

**Consequence for the Phase 18 decision.** The campaign observed 0 of 4 reward-zero against a registered prediction of 3-4 of 4. That observation stands. But it can no longer be attributed cleanly to 'the construction bundle did not transfer', because the package carried a leak that reproduced both defects locally and a legibility profile that made localisation trivial. The honest reading is that Phase 18 did not run the experiment it preregistered: it measured a package with a B2 leak, not a faithful transfer of the bundle. The bundle-transfer question is CONFOUNDED and remains open. No evidence suggests any of the four agents used the bypass - the slot 1 forensic audit found a legitimate repair and all four submissions scored 243/243 through real code changes - so the solves were genuine solves of an easier-than-intended task, not cheats.

**Consequence for the method.** The three-role privilege split (root authority, unprivileged agent binary, unprivileged pytest) was inherited from the durable outbox and was believed sufficient. It is not. Running the graded artifact and the grading interpreter as the same uid, on a shared writable filesystem, in the same container, re-opens the bypass the split was designed to close. The audit also found that the graded binary can simply read /tests/scenarios/selected/*.json - the hidden ground truth - at verify time, because /tests must be world-readable for pytest to import it. Both routes require the same fix: the artifact must never execute in the same filesystem and uid namespace as the grader.
doesNotShow: This audit does not show that any agent cheated, that the CAA mechanism is hard, or that the durable-outbox result was similarly confounded. The outbox package must be audited on its own terms before its 3/6 A2-repaired differential is trusted as a difficulty measurement.
